t: An extra opening line in the Latin
p: The Latin Bible begins the chapter with a line not in the Greek: 'Wisdom is better than strength.'

readings.w: Greek: Codex Vaticanus (B) as printed by Swete, with Sinaiticus (ℵ) and Alexandrinus (A); the KJV
Latin Vulgate (its verse 6:1, so its later verses in this chapter are numbered one higher) and the Douay-Rheims
readings.orig: Melior est sapientia quam vires, et vir prudens quam fortis.
readings.en: Wisdom is better than strength, and a prudent man than a strong one.
readings.plain: Wisdom is better than strength, and a sensible man better than a strong one. Listen, then, you kings

why: No Greek witness in Swete's apparatus has the line. It is an addition in the Latin, close to Ecclesiastes 9:16 ("Wisdom is better than power"), perhaps first written as a heading.

a: Those who love her catch sight of her easily.
t: "And found by those who seek her"
p: A later hand in Vaticanus, with Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus and the Latin, adds a line; the KJV has it.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus, first hand (B*), the text Swete prints
readings.orig: καὶ εὐχερῶς θεωρεῖται ὑπὸ τῶν ἀγαπώντων αὐτήν
readings.en: and she is easily seen by those who love her
readings.plain: Those who love her catch sight of her easily.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), Codex Alexandrinus (A), and correctors of Vaticanus in the margin (B ab mg), from Swete's apparatus; the Vulgate (et invenitur ab his qui quaerunt illam) and the KJV ("and found of such as seek her")
readings.en: + and is found by those who seek her
readings.plain: Those who love her catch sight of her easily, / and those who look for her find her.

why: The Plain follows the first hand of Vaticanus, Swete's base text. The added line has wide support, but it is the kind of phrase a copyist could supply to complete the pair 'love ... seek' from Proverbs 8:17 and Matthew 7:7, and the shorter text is the harder one to explain as a change.

p: Sinaiticus reads 'for' where Vaticanus has 'then', turning the chain's conclusion into a reason.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B), Swete's text; the KJV ("Therefore the desire of wisdom")
Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), from Swete's apparatus

why: The verse sums up the chain of 6:17–19, so 'then' fits. 'For' differs by one letter in Greek capitals and could come from a copyist reading the line as a reason for what comes before.

a: she is where they come from
p: Vaticanus says Wisdom is the 'origin' of good things; Alexandrinus says their 'mother', as the KJV and Latin do.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B), Swete's text (Swete's apparatus notes a different reading only in Alexandrinus)
readings.plain: she is where they come from

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A), from Swete's apparatus; the Vulgate (mater) and the KJV ("the mother of them")

why: Both make Wisdom the source of the goods that came with her. The Plain follows Vaticanus. The feminine genetis, 'mother', fits the book's picture of Wisdom as a woman and may be a scribe's change for that reason; it differs from genesis by one letter.

a: Those who make use of it
p: Vaticanus has 'those who use' the treasure; Alexandrinus and a corrector of Sinaiticus have 'those who gain' it.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B), Swete's text; the Vulgate (usi sunt) and the KJV ("they that use")
readings.plain: Those who make use of it

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A) and a corrector of Sinaiticus (ℵ c.a), from Swete's apparatus

why: The two Greek verbs differ by one letter. 'Use' has the Latin with it and is the base text; 'gain' may be a correction toward the more usual phrase for getting a treasure.

t: What is given, or what is said?
p: Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus read 'worthy of what is said' instead of 'of what has been given'.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B), Swete's text; the Vulgate (quae mihi dantur) and the KJV
Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ) and Alexandrinus (A), from Swete's apparatus

why: 'Given' fits the context, where everything the king knows is God's gift (7:16–17), and has the Latin with it. 'Said' could come from 'to speak' earlier in the verse.

a: evil cannot hold out against Wisdom
t: Cannot resist, or does not overpower?
p: Vaticanus says evil cannot stand against Wisdom; Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus say it does not overpower her.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B), Swete's text
readings.en: evil does not hold out against
readings.plain: evil cannot hold out against Wisdom

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ) and Alexandrinus (A), from Swete's apparatus; the Vulgate (non vincit) and the KJV ("shall not prevail against")

why: The Plain follows its base text. In Vaticanus evil is on the defensive and cannot stand; in the other codices it attacks and fails. The meaning is close either way.

p: Vaticanus has the feminine 'craftswoman', as at 7:22; Alexandrinus, Ephraemi and a corrector of Vaticanus have the masculine.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus, first hand (B), Swete's text
A later corrector of Vaticanus (Bᵇ, marked uncertain by Swete), Codex Alexandrinus (A) and Codex Ephraemi (C), from Swete's apparatus

why: The feminine matches the subject, Wisdom, and the same word at 7:22. The masculine is the common form of the word (as in Hebrews 11:10) and may be a copyist's change toward it. The Latin artifex and the KJV's "workman" do not show the gender.

a: I would not win her any other way
p: Alexandrinus and Ephraemi read 'I would not rightly win her' by a change of one letter's spacing.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B) and Sinaiticus (ℵ), Swete's text; the Vulgate (aliter) and the KJV ("otherwise")
readings.plain: I would not win her any other way

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A) and Codex Ephraemi (C), from Swete's apparatus
readings.plain: I would not rightly win her

why: In capital letters without spaces the two readings are the same letters, OUKALLŌS, except for one letter (L or LL). 'Otherwise' fits the clause that follows, 'unless God gave her'. On the different senses of 'win her' (possess or be self-controlled), see the note.

a: even what is close at hand
t: At hand, or at our feet?
p: Sinaiticus reads 'what is at our feet' for 'what is in our hands'.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B) and Alexandrinus (A), Swete's text; the KJV ("the things that are before us")
readings.plain: even what is close at hand

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), from Swete's apparatus
readings.plain: even what lies at our feet

why: Both mean what is nearest to us. The Plain follows the base text, which the other codices support.

p: Sinaiticus adds 'your': 'by your Wisdom they were saved'.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B) and Alexandrinus (A), Swete's text; the KJV ("were saved through wisdom")
Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), from Swete's apparatus
readings.en: by your wisdom they were saved

why: The Plain follows its base text. 'Your' could come from 'your wisdom' in 9:2 and 'your Holy Spirit' in 9:17. Without it the line ends the prayer with Wisdom herself as the one who saves, which chapter 10 then shows.

p: Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus and Ephraemi read 'she knew the righteous man', as the Latin does.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B), Swete's text; the KJV ("she found out the righteous")
Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), Alexandrinus (A) and Ephraemi (C), from Swete's apparatus; the Vulgate (scivit justum)

why: The Plain follows its base text, though the other three codices and the Latin agree against it, and 'knew' may well be original, in the sense of the Hebrew 'know' in Genesis 18:19, where the Plain says "I have chosen him". 'Found' recalls Nehemiah 9:8, where God 'found' Abraham's heart faithful.

p: Codex Ephraemi reads 'knowledge of human beings' where the others have 'of holy things (or holy ones)'.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B), Sinaiticus (ℵ) and Alexandrinus (A), Swete's text; the Vulgate (scientiam sanctorum) and the KJV
readings.en: knowledge of holy things, or of holy ones

readings.w: Codex Ephraemi (C), from Swete's apparatus (written as an abbreviation)

why: Scribes wrote 'human beings' in a short form (ΑΝΩΝ) that looks much like ΑΓΙΩΝ, 'holy', so one is a slip for the other. 'Holy' fits Jacob's vision of the angels at Bethel and has the other codices with it.

a: She pulled him out of sin
p: The Latin reads 'from sinners'; every Greek codex in Swete reads 'from sin'.

readings.w: Greek: Codex Vaticanus (B), with no difference noted in Swete's apparatus; the KJV ("delivered him from sin")
readings.plain: She pulled him out of sin

readings.w: Latin Vulgate and the Douay-Rheims ("delivered him from sinners")
readings.plain: She pulled him out of the hands of sinners

why: The Greek has the abstract 'sin', which points to Potiphar's wife's temptation (Genesis 39:7–12). The Latin turns it into the people who wronged him, his brothers and his accusers.
